knownFor: The drowning of Magnus Eriksson at Lyngholmen on 1 December 1374
A position on the leia, the sheltered coastal shipping lane of western Norway
Moster and its twelfth-century stone church
overview: A western Norwegian island municipality on the main coastal sailing route, where Magnus Eriksson was drowned in 1374.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Bømlo is not one island but around nine hundred islands, islets and skerries in southern Vestland, lying north of the entrance to the Hardangerfjord. The main island gives the municipality its name, and the waters around it — the Bømlafjorden and the sounds between the skerries — carry the main north-south sea route along the Norwegian coast.

In a country where until modern times almost all travel of any distance went by water, that made this an unavoidable stretch of road rather than a remote archipelago. Kings, bishops, traders and fleets passed through it, and one king did not get past it.

contentSections.title: The shipping lane
paragraphs: The Norwegian coast is sheltered from the open Atlantic by a nearly continuous chain of islands, and the passage inside them — the leia — allowed medieval ships to run the length of the country in relative safety. Bømlo sits on that route at the point where vessels coming south from Bergen must cross the mouth of the Hardangerfjord.

Shelter is relative. The channels are narrow, studded with skerries that barely break the surface, and swept by tides and winter storms, and a December passage in an open-decked medieval ship was a serious undertaking. The sailing conditions here are the reason Bømlo appears in the record at all.

contentSections.title: Moster
paragraphs: The island of Moster, part of the municipality, carries a small stone church of the twelfth century — one of the oldest churches in Norway, and a substantial thing to find in a fishing community of this size. Its presence says something about the traffic passing the island: a stone church needed patrons and a reason.

Moster is also the centre of Norwegian tradition about the coming of Christianity to the country, and the arrival of the new religion by sea is staged there each summer in an open-air play, the Mostraspelet. The play is a modern institution rather than a medieval one, and the traditions it dramatises belong to saga literature written down long after the events, but the church is real and early.

contentSections.title: The drowning of Magnus Eriksson, 1374
paragraphs: Magnus Eriksson had been king of Sweden and of Norway, and had lost both. He was deposed in Sweden in 1364 in favour of Albert of Mecklenburg, spent years in captivity, and was released in 1371 when his son Haakon VI paid twelve thousand marks for him. He lived his last years in Norway under his son’s protection, a king without a kingdom.

On 1 December 1374 he was sailing from Bergen towards eastern Norway when his ship ran aground at Lyngholmen, off the Bømlafjorden, and he was drowned. The Icelandic annals record the wreck, which is how the date is known, and the loss of a former king of two kingdoms in a coastal accident is exactly the kind of event the annals were good at registering and bad at describing: there is no account of how it happened.

contentSections.title: A king with no grave
paragraphs: Magnus and his wife Blanche had asked in their testament of 1347 to be buried at Vadstena, the house in Sweden that Birgitta founded, but by 1374 the politics made that impossible and the wish was not honoured. Where he was actually buried is not known; the church of St Mary in Oslo has been suggested, without proof. For a man who wore two crowns, the absence of a grave is striking.

The vacuum drew stories. A later Russian chronicle claimed that Magnus survived the wreck and ended his life as a monk in the Novgorod lands, a tale with no support in the Scandinavian record and treated as apocryphal. The bare facts remain a wreck on a December night among the skerries, and a king who went into the water off Bømlo.

name: Bømlo
summary: An island group at the mouth of the Hardangerfjord on Norway’s coastal shipping lane, where Magnus Eriksson drowned in a wreck at Lyngholmen on 1 December 1374.

imageInfo.caption: The coast at Bremnes on Bømlo in western Norway, photographed in 2013.
imageInfo.creator: Frokor
imageInfo.note: A landscape photograph of the island coast: the low skerries and narrow sounds in the picture are the sailing conditions that wrecked the king’s ship in 1374. No medieval depiction of the place exists.

timeline.description: His son Haakon VI pays twelve thousand marks to free him, and Magnus settles in Norway.

timeline.title: Wrecked at Lyngholmen
timeline.description: Sailing from Bergen towards eastern Norway, Magnus Eriksson’s ship grounds off the Bømlafjorden and he is drowned; the Icelandic annals record it.

timeline.title: No known grave
timeline.description: The burial place is unrecorded; the request in his testament of 1347 to lie at Vadstena was not fulfilled.
